title: Episode 77: Trending — People prefer to negotiate with women, even when outcomes are identical and gender is unknown
itunes_title: Trending — People prefer to negotiate with women, even when outcomes are identical and gender is unknown
description:
**Top Trending Friday** — our weekly pick of the top-trending paper on r/science this week.

**Paper:** [People prefer to negotiate with women, even when outcomes are identical and gender is unknown](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2523202123)

**Authors:** Charlotte H. Townsend, Laura J. Kray, Solène Delecourt

**Journal:** Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 2026

**Why it matters:** Decades of negotiation research have focused on who wins the most money, but this paper shows that the social and emotional quality of a negotiation — and its compounding career consequences — may matter just as much.

**Summary**

Negotiation research has long prioritized *economic* outcomes (who captured the most value) while largely ignoring *subjective* outcomes: trust built, perceived fairness, and the counterpart's desire to negotiate again. This paper, drawing on over 2,000 observations, finds that people consistently report higher subjective value when negotiating with women — and that this preference survives even complete anonymization. In a text-chat study using a fictitious resource-allocation task, gender was so effectively hidden that third-party observers reading the transcripts guessed the negotiator's gender correctly only 43% of the time — statistically worse than a coin flip — yet participants still preferred their women counterparts on subjective measures. Crucially, women achieved identical distributive and integrative economic outcomes to men across all conditions.

To uncover the behavioral mechanism, the researchers fed anonymous transcripts through a natural language processing model trained to classify negotiation utterances into 12 behavioral codes. Women were significantly more likely to make multi-issue offers and to accept offers — a pattern that might look like capitulation but functioned as *strategic validation*: yielding on lower-priority points while holding firm on overall economic value, leaving counterparts feeling heard without sacrificing outcomes. A Monte Carlo simulation then modeled what happens when a modest 2.5-percentage-point difference in willingness to re-engage compounds over a career: women accumulated roughly 44–56% more negotiation opportunities, translating a subjective edge into a substantial long-term earnings gap. One important caveat: all studies used low-ambiguity settings where negotiation was explicit; prior work suggests women can face economic and social penalties when the appropriateness of negotiating is itself unclear.

**Three takeaways**

1. People rated subjective value — liking, trust, and desire to negotiate again — significantly higher with women partners even in fully anonymous text negotiations where gender could not be inferred from behavior.
2. AI-coded transcripts identified two specific behaviors driving the effect: women made multi-issue offers and accepted offers at higher rates, yet still achieved the same economic point totals as men, indicating strategic rather than costly yielding.
3. A Monte Carlo simulation based on observed re-engagement probabilities (94.4% vs. 91.9%) projected that women would accumulate ~44–56% more negotiation opportunities over time, compounding into roughly $55,000 more in simulated career earnings under identical per-deal performance.

**Read the source:** https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2523202123

source_metadata.abstract: While gender and economic outcomes in negotiation have been studied for decades, much less is known about gender differences in subjective outcomes, such as trust, rapport, and willingness to negotiate again, despite their importance for long-term success. In a series of studies with over 2,000 participants, we find that people consistently report better subjective outcomes when negotiating with women. This preference persists even in anonymous negotiations where gender is unknown and cannot be inferred from behavior, as well as in conditions where negotiation partner gender is randomly assigned. Importantly, we find no gender difference in economic outcomes. To understand why, we analyzed transcripts of real negotiations for any behavioral differences. These findings reveal an overlooked gender dynamic: While men and women achieve similar economic results, women foster stronger interpersonal relationships, which in turn lead to greater satisfaction and greater desire for future negotiations with women.
